title: Chapter 228 – The Library of Names
html:
[Terrace Eight – Yue]

The stair ends in a door of paper.

Yue stops at the top of it with her stone hand raised, and for a moment she does not understand what she is looking at. It is a tall door, twice her height, set in a wall of gray stone, and it is made of a thousand thousand sheets of paper laid one upon another and bound with red thread. Each sheet is written on. She can see the ink, small and black and tidy, line upon line, in a script she has never learned. It is the smell that reaches her first: dust and glue and old leather and cold ash, the smell of a place where things are kept.

"A library," says Hua, softly, behind her.

"Of course it is," says Yue. "It rustled all the way up."

She puts her hand against the paper.

It is warm. It gives under her palm like cloth. And then, with a dry soft sound like the turning of a page, it parts, down the middle, and the two halves fold back against the wall, and a long dim vaulted room opens before them, lit by the light of a thousand candles.

---

It is the largest room she has ever seen.

It is not a room at all, she decides, after a moment's staring. It is a country. The ceiling is lost in shadow, a hundred feet up or more, and between the floor and the dark rise shelves: tall black shelves of some polished wood, row on row, aisle on aisle, running away to every horizon. Every shelf is full. Every shelf holds books. They are small books, no bigger than a hand, bound in plain gray cloth, each with a single narrow paper label on the spine. There are millions of them. There are more than she can count. And in the narrow aisles between the shelves, small and bright and steady, hang the candles.

They float. They have no holders. They hang in the air at the height of a man's shoulder, each a tiny point of gold, and when she walks between them they drift aside, politely, like cats.

"What is it?" says Pebble, in a whisper.

"The Eighth," says Veyra. Her voice is faint but steady. She leans on Corin's thin arm, and her face in the candlelight is the gray of old ash. "The Archive. Every name that was ever paid."

"Paid?"

Given up. She draws a slow breath. Taken, surrendered, bartered, forgotten. Every name the Road has cost its passengers. They come here. They are shelved. She lifts a hand and lets it fall. It is the only mercy the Founders built.

Yue looks at the nearest shelf.

The labels are written in the common tongue, thank the Heavens, in a small clear hand. She reads the first. HESTER VANE, daughter of a baker, aged eleven, Second Landing. She reads the second. THOMAS OAK, a drover, Fourth Landing, in exchange for his brother's cough. The third. The fourth. The fifth.

Mara. Dom. Little Ket. Aldous. The woman with the red shawl.

"These are the ones who paid," she says.

"Yes."

"They're all here."

"Every one."

"Then why don't they come back?"

They cannot. Veyra's voice is very low. A name that is shelved is a name that is safe. The Bloom cannot read what is in the Archive. It is the only place it cannot go. A pause. And the Keeper will not let anyone take them down.

"Keeper?" says Yue.

"That," says a voice, "would be me."

---

The woman sitting at the end of the aisle is seventy years old, and she has been seventy for six hundred.

She sits at a small writing desk, under a hanging candle, with a quill in her hand and a ledger open before her. She is a plump, brisk, comfortable person in a gray linen smock with ink on the cuffs, with a round weathered face and a great deal of white hair pinned up in a careless knot, from which a second quill protrudes at a rakish angle. She wears spectacles. They have been mended with thread. She looks up as they approach, over the top of them, and her bright black eyes go quickly from face to face, and a slow warm smile spreads over her features.

"Well," she says. "Look at that. Nine days early."

Nobody answers.

"I did say it'd be nine," says the woman, to herself. She pushes her spectacles up her nose. "I did say. I put it in the note. Ma Ruo-lin, I said, they'll come up by the ninth of the Wall's month, and you'll have your tea ready." She beams. "And here you are. Sit down. Sit down, all of you. I haven't got enough chairs, but I've got a very large floor."

"Ma Ruo-lin," says Jian, slowly.

He has gone very pale.

"That's right, dear." She sets down her quill. "You'll be the one with the machine."

The note, thinks Yue. COME UP.

She had heard of it. Everyone had. A scrap of paper, found at the end of Arc Six, tucked under a stone in the Hall's last archive, written in a small cramped hand: DOOR TEN. COME UP. M.R.L. They had stood around it for an hour, arguing about whether it was a trap. Jian had said nothing. He had folded it carefully and put it in his sleeve. And now, six hundred years and eight Terraces later, the writer sits at her desk in a gray linen smock, with a quill stuck in her hair, offering tea.

"You wrote it," Jian says.

"Of course I did." Ma Ruo-lin looks pleased. "Who else? I was the Hall's senior archivist for forty years. I climbed up here myself when the old Keeper died. It seemed rude to leave the place empty." She taps the ledger. "I've been running it ever since. It's very restful. Nobody shouts."

"You knew we were coming."

"I've known for a year. By the Hall's reckoning." Her smile widens. "The Library is quite sensitive. When a new name is read in a place it shouldn't be, I hear about it. And a name that was read on the Wall, at the Mending, and then again in the Orchard, and then again on the Loom—" She shakes her head. "Well. One notices. I'm an archivist. It's what we do."

Jian says, very carefully: "You know my name."

"I know your names." She looks at him over the spectacles, and her eyes are bright and kind and unmistakably shrewd. "Both of them. Or all three. I never cared to count." A pause. "I'm sorry, dear. It's a terrible indelicacy. I shouldn't have brought it up. Let's have tea."

---

They drink it on the floor, in a circle, between two great shelves, with the candles hanging overhead like a ceiling of low gold stars.

The tea is excellent. It is strong and black and sweet, and it comes in plain white cups from a dented tin pot that Ma Ruo-lin produces from a drawer. There are biscuits. Yue eats four. She had not known she was hungry, and the hunger comes on her all at once, like a wave, and she realizes with a small shock that it is the first time in eight Terraces that she has been able to taste.

"You've been paying heavily," Ma Ruo-lin observes, watching her.

"We all have."

"Yes, but you've paid in the senses." She taps her own tongue. "The Road takes it from you, bit by bit. Taste. Warmth. Hearing. It's all stored here, in the lower stacks. If you wish to get it back, I could look."

"No," says Yue.

"No?"

"I don't want it back." She sets down her cup. "I chose it. If I take it back, it was never a choice."

The old archivist looks at her for a long moment. Then she nods, slowly, and picks up a biscuit.

"I used to feel that way," she says. "I gave up my eyes, you know. When I came up the Road. Both of them, at the Fifth. I thought it was a fair trade." She chews. "Then I came here, and the old Keeper handed me a pair of spectacles, and said, there's a thing called a lens." She smiles. "They're not very good eyes. But they're mine. I'd forgotten that a thing could be both a cost and a gift."

"You can see?"

"With these on? Perfectly well."

Hua laughs.

It is a small startled sound, but it relaxes the whole circle. Pebble grins. Even Corin's thin face loosens, a little, and Ye Shuhan, who lies propped against a stack of books with a blanket over his knees, gives a feeble snort.

I like her, thinks Yue, with some surprise.

---

"I'll tell you what I know," says Ma Ruo-lin, "and then I'll tell you what you need to do, and then I'll give you a bed, because you look as though you've been dragged through a hedge."

She has refilled the cups. She sits with her legs crossed and her ledger in her lap, like a schoolmistress, and she speaks in a brisk even tone, without pausing for effect, as if reading from a list.

"The Door is a round room. You've heard about it. Nine seats, glass roof, the Seam overhead. Orrin Thann sits in the ninth. He's been there six hundred years. He isn't dead, and he isn't alive, and he isn't entirely himself." She sips. "He's been shouting for the last month, by our time. Not aloud. Down the Road. Through the Terraces. Through the stones. He wants the Nine."

"The Nine," says Yue.

"The Ring. The people who share the burden." Ma Ruo-lin's bright eyes rest on Jian. "He's sent for them. He's been calling their names. I can hear it, down here, in the books. It comes through the walls like a bell."

"Which names?"

"Yours." She nods at Jian. "Hers." Yue. "Hers." Hua. "The boy's." Pebble. "And five more. A woman called Mei. A man called Cheng Hui. A woman called Hai Ren. A man called Tian Mo. A girl called Mo Yan."

Yue's blood goes cold.

"Mo Yan," she says.

"Yes."

"She's on the Wall. She's fifty-eight. She's—"

"She left the Wall two days ago." The archivist consults a page. "She's on the Hundred Stairs. She's about to enter the Quay of Bells. She'll be at the Fifth Terrace tonight, and the Sixth by dawn. The time-ratios will catch her up. She'll be here in a week."

"A week?"

"By our reckoning." Ma Ruo-lin smiles. "The Eighth runs one to one. The ones below run fast. It's the quiet Terrace. You can do a great deal of living here, and nobody notices."

Pebble has gone white.

"And Sun?" he says.

The old woman's smile fades.

"I'm sorry, dear." She turns a page. "I haven't got your sister. She's in the warp. She's one of the two million. She isn't shelved. She's woven." She looks up. "But I have her name."

"Her name?"

"The Archive keeps every name that was spoken, in the end. The ones in the warp aren't gone. They're held." She closes the ledger gently. "If you can get to the Door, and cut the warp, and hold the ninth seat for long enough, you can call her back. I don't know if you can. But the name is here."

Pebble puts his face in his hands.

Yue, beside him, reaches out and lays her stone hand on his shaved head. She does not speak. She has nothing to say. After a moment, she feels his shoulders shake, once, and still.

---

Jian asks about the Tenth while the second pot is brewing.

He asks it quietly, with his eyes on the steam, and Yue sees Ma Ruo-lin's hands go still on the lid. The candles nearest the circle drift a little closer, as if they too are listening.

"The machine," says the old archivist. "Yes. I wondered when."

"Orrin wore it."

"For a month." She sets the lid down. "Not a day more. It was the Draughtswoman's design, you understand, and she built it for nine hands to share. It was never meant to sit on one. Orrin put it on because the other eight were dead, or gone, or too far from the Door to answer. He was the youngest of the Founders and the only one who still believed the Seam could be held by a single will." She shakes her head. "It ate him. Not all at once. A little each night, the way damp eats a wall."

"And then it left him."

"It was taken." Her voice sharpens. "That is the part the Hall never wrote down. The Tenth did not slip off Orrin like a cloak. Something reached into the Door and pulled it free, and half of it went with the thief, and the other half stayed in the room. The half that stayed is the one you carry." She looks at him over the mended spectacles. "The half that went is the one the Bloom wears."

Jian does not move.

Yue watches his face. She has learned to read it over the years, the way a sailor reads a sky: the tight stillness of the jaw, the long blink, the careful way he lets his breath go. He is afraid. He has not said so, and he will not, but she sees the fear sitting behind his eyes like a lamp behind a shutter.

"Then the Bloom is not whole," says Hua.

"No. It is half a machine wearing half a god, and it knows it." Ma Ruo-lin pours. "That is why it wants the Door. It cannot finish itself anywhere else. And that is why Orrin shouts. He cannot finish either. He sits in the ninth seat with his hands on the arms and he cannot get up, because if he gets up the room is empty and the Seam closes over it, and the Bloom walks in."

"He is holding the door," says Yue slowly.

"With his teeth. For six hundred years."

Nobody drinks.

"What does he want from us?" asks Pebble.

"A relief." The archivist's voice softens. "Nine hands, sitting in nine seats. That is the whole of the Founders' design, child. Nobody was ever supposed to carry it alone. He wants to stand up, at last, and walk out of that room, and be allowed to be tired."

Be allowed to be tired, thinks Yue.

She looks across the circle at Jian, who has bent his head over his cup. She knows what he is doing. He is doing the sum. Nine seats. Five names at the bottom of the page. Four in this circle. One climbing the Hundred Stairs at fifty-eight years old with a bad knee and a stubborn heart.

"It is a price," he says finally.

"Everything here is."

"Name it."

Ma Ruo-lin hesitates, and the hesitation is the first unkind thing Yue has seen her do.

"Whoever sits," she says, "does not leave. Not as Orrin has not left. The seat holds you as long as you hold it, and the Seam does not care how long that is. The Founders drew lots and rotated, one season each, because no one could bear more." She turns the cup in her hands. "Nine seats. Nine hands. A season apiece. It works, if all nine are there. If one is missing, the rest must carry the gap."

"And if two are missing?"

"Then someone sits for two seasons. And someone else for three." She does not look up. "And so on, until the Ring is whole or the sitters are not."

The candles hang quite still.

"Then we find all nine," says Jian.

"Yes."

"And we do not lose any."

Ma Ruo-lin lifts her eyes. They are bright and tired and very old, and Yue sees in them something she has not seen in a face since her own mother's, the look of someone who has watched many brave people say exactly that sentence.

"Dear," she says gently, "I hope so."

---

The old archivist shows them the lower stacks before the naming, because she says it will help.

It is a long walk. The aisles narrow and darken as they descend a spiral stair of black wood, and the candles thin out until there is only one to each turning. The books change. Down here they are older, and their labels are not names but things: The sound of her mother's voice. The smell of rain on the east wall. Seven summers. A brother's laugh.

"The senses," says Yue.

"And memories. And loves." Ma Ruo-lin's lantern swings ahead of her. "Everything the Road has taken that was not a name. It is all here. None of it is lost."

"You said that already."

"I say it to everyone. It is the only comfort I have." She stops at a shelf and runs one finger along a spine. "I keep it dusted."

Yue looks at the thousand gray backs, and thinks of Pebble's sister, and of the two million woven into the Door's warp, and of the red thread on the Loom. She thinks of a hand made of stone. She thinks that of everything she has seen on the Road, this quiet cellar of kept things is the one that frightens her most, because it is a kindness, and she does not know what it will cost.

"What did you pay for the spectacles?" she asks.

The old woman laughs, short and surprised.

"Nothing," she says. "They were a gift." She taps the thread-mended frame. "That was the first lesson I learned in this place. Some things are free. You just have to be willing to be handed them."

She does not say who handed her the spectacles. Yue does not ask. But she notices, climbing the stair back toward the candlelight, that Ma Ruo-lin touches the frame once, lightly, with two fingers, as one touches the hand of someone who is gone.

---

"Now," says Ma Ruo-lin. "The naming."

She says it briskly, as one moves on to the next item in a list. She has stood up, with a creak of knees, and gone to a high shelf, and taken down a small wooden box. She sets it on the floor in the center of the circle, and opens it. Inside, on a bed of gray wool, lie four small white stones, each no bigger than an egg.

"You've got infants," she says. "Haven't you? I can smell it from here. The Loom did its work. Three of you, at least." She counts. "Four? The boy's still Core. Three, then. And you'll want to get them born before the Door."

"We were told they need a sky," says Hua.

"They do. They also need a name." The old woman sits back on her heels. "A Soul without a name is a Soul that anyone can call. The Bloom's been collecting names since before the Road was built. It's got a very large hand. If you carry a Soul to the Door unnamed, it'll be gone before the first cloud."

"Then we name them."

"That's the rite." Ma Ruo-lin lifts a stone. "It isn't hard. You give each Soul a name. Not the name you were born with. A new one. A true one. And it has to be given by someone else."

"Someone else?"

"Someone who loves you. Or who's tied to you. Or who has no reason to want you dead." She turns the stone in her fingers. "It can't be self-named. The Bloom can hear a self-named name from three Terraces away. But a name given by another, in a low voice, in this room, is as good as buried."

"What does it cost?"

"The one who names carries it." She says it plainly. "In their heart. Not on paper. Not in a book. It lives in their memory, and nowhere else. If they die, the name dies with them, and the Soul is nameless again."

Silence.

"That's the weakness," says Ma Ruo-lin. "I won't pretend otherwise. You're binding two lives together. If one goes, the other's in danger." She sets the stone back in the box. "But it's also the strength. A Soul whose name is guarded by a friend can be brought back from the edge of anything."

Yue looks at the four white stones.

She does the sum without effort. There are four of them: Jian, Yue, Hua, Pebble. Three infants and a Core. The old woman said three. There are four names to be given, three of them now, and one soon, and each name to be held in a different heart. It is a circle. It is a closed ring. It is, she realizes, the oldest and simplest form of the Ring they have lost.

Of course, she thinks. It was always going to be a circle.

---

They do it that night.

The old archivist lays out four mats on the floor, in the lee of the great shelf, and lights four candles, and tells them to sit. She does not make a ceremony of it. She sits at the edge of the circle with her ledger on her knee, and watches, with a mild proprietary air, as the four of them arrange themselves.

Jian sits across from Yue.

He has not spoken since the biscuits. His face, in the candlelight, is lean and tired and absolutely calm. He holds one of the white stones in his steady hand, and as she watches he closes his fingers over it and lets out a long slow breath.

"I'll name you," she says.

It comes out before she has decided. Her own voice startles her. She sees Jian's head lift, and the quick bright flicker of surprise in his eyes, and she thinks: I should have asked.

"If you wish," he says.

"I do."

"It is a heavy thing to carry."

"I've carried heavier." She leans forward. "Give me your hand."

He does. It is warm, and dry, and perfectly still. She holds it in her own right hand, and the stone between them, and she closes her eyes and thinks of every word she knows for what he is.

Healer. Liar. Brother. Stranger. Thief. Friend.

None of them is right.

A man who stands in a door, she thinks, and does not let it close.

"I name you Threshold," she says, very low.

Jian does not move.

The stone in their joined hands goes warm. It brightens. A thin gold light runs up through the white, and into his fingers, and up his arm, and she feels something turn over in her chest, a small hard click, like a key finding its lock.

"Threshold," he whispers.

"Don't say it again."

"No."

"I'll keep it."

"Yes." His voice is rough. "I know you will."

Beside them Hua is laughing and weeping at once, her face bright with candlelight, as Jian's low voice gives her a word that Yue cannot hear. Pebble sits very straight with his hand in Hua's, whispering something, his lips moving, his eyes shut. And Yue, in the center of the circle, feels a small cold hand take her stone one, and a thin steady voice say, in her ear:

"I name you Hold."

She turns.

The boy is kneeling in front of her. His face is bright with tears. In his hand there is a white stone, glowing gold, and his other hand is wrapped round her wrist, and she sees that he has been planning it for a very long time.

"Hold," she says.

"It's what you do." His voice shakes. "It's what you've always done. You hold. The line. The gate. Everyone." He swallows. "You hold us. I wanted you to have a name that said so."

She cannot speak.

"I'll keep it," he says. "I'll keep it as long as I live."

As long as you live, she thinks.

She remembers the red thread on the Loom, long and bright and unending. She remembers the old Keeper's voice: longer than the Door. Longer than the Seam. She looks into the boy's wet face, with its bruised steady eyes, and understands, for the first time, exactly what she is being given.

A hundred years. Two hundred. A name, carried in a living heart, long after the rest of her has gone to dust.

"Pebble," she says.

"Master?"

"Thank you."

He bursts into tears.

She holds him. It is awkward; her stone hand is stiff, and he is all knees and elbows, and the candles hang overhead like a ring of small gold suns. She holds him anyway. And over his shoulder she sees Ma Ruo-lin, at the edge of the circle, with her quill poised and her spectacles gleaming, writing something very small and neat on a page of her ledger.

What are you writing? Yue thinks, to nobody.

The old archivist looks up. She meets her eyes across the candlelit dark. And she smiles, a little sadly, and tilts the ledger so that Yue can read it.

At the top of the page, in a small cramped hand, are four names.

At the bottom, beneath them, are five more.
